subjects.name: Lion

An orange big cat with bold black stripes, like Shere Khan in The Jungle Book.

subjects.name: African Elephant

clues: A newborn cub weighs only about 100 grams, roughly as much as an apple.
An enlarged wrist bone works like an extra thumb for gripping stalks.

A black-and-white bear from China that feeds almost only on bamboo.

subjects.name: Giraffe

The tallest animal on Earth, with a very long neck for reaching treetops.
subjects.fact: A tall male can stand around 5.5 metres high.

subjects.name: Polar Bear
clues: Under its thick fur, its skin is actually black.
Its fur hairs are not truly white but see-through, scattering light to look pale.

The great white bear of the Arctic, found in Canada, Greenland and Svalbard.

subjects.fact: It is usually described as the largest land carnivore alive today.

Large males sometimes 'box', kicking and pushing to settle disputes.

Australia's famous hopping marsupial, which carries its joey in a pouch.

subjects.name: Koala
clues: It sleeps or rests for up to about 20 hours a day.
Its diet is so low in energy that it spends most of its time resting.
Like humans, it has fingerprints that are very hard to tell from our own.
It feeds almost entirely on the leaves of eucalyptus trees.
A fluffy grey tree-dwelling marsupial from Australia, often wrongly called a bear.
subjects.fact: Its baby, called a joey, stays in its mother's pouch for about six months.

subjects.name: Gorilla
clues: It shares about 98% of its DNA with humans.
It builds a fresh nest of leaves to sleep in almost every night.
It usually walks on all fours, leaning on its knuckles.
Its mountain form lives in volcanic forests of Rwanda, Uganda and DR Congo.
The largest of all apes, whose leading adult male is called a silverback.
subjects.fact: A silverback gets its name from the patch of silvery hair that grows on an adult male's back.

subjects.name: Cheetah
clues: Unlike other big cats, it cannot fully pull in its claws, which grip like running spikes.
Dark 'tear marks' run from the corners of its eyes to its mouth.

It is a close relative of the horse and the donkey.
Huge herds migrate across the Serengeti alongside wildebeest.
A horse-like animal of the savanna with black-and-white stripes.
subjects.fact: Under its striped coat, its skin is dark.

subjects.name: Hippopotamus
clues: Its name comes from Ancient Greek words meaning 'river horse'.
Its closest living relatives are whales and dolphins.
Its skin gives off a reddish oily fluid that works like sunscreen.
It spends its days in rivers and lakes and comes out at night to graze.

It closes its eyes, ears and nose every time it dives.
It is one of very few mammals that lay eggs.
An Australian animal with a duck-like bill, webbed feet and a beaver-like tail.

subjects.name: Grey Wolf
clues: It is the closest wild relative of the pet dog.

The largest wild member of the dog family, famous for its eerie howl.

subjects.name: Bald Eagle

It often steals fish from ospreys instead of catching its own.

Once harmed badly by the pesticide DDT, it has made a strong comeback.
A white-headed bird of prey and the national bird of the United States.

subjects.name: Emperor Penguin
clues: It can dive deeper than 500 metres and hold its breath for over 20 minutes.
It breeds in the middle of winter, when temperatures can drop below minus 40.

Thousands huddle together, taking turns in the warm middle to survive blizzards.
The largest of the tuxedo-wearing flightless birds, living only in Antarctica.
subjects.fact: It can stand over a metre tall and weigh more than 30 kg.

subjects.name: Ostrich
clues: Each of its eyes is bigger than its brain.
It has only two toes on each foot, fewer than any other bird.
Its powerful forward kick can seriously injure a predator.

The world's largest bird, a fast flightless runner of the savanna.
subjects.fact: It can sprint at about 70 km/h, faster than any other bird on land.

subjects.name: Flamingo
clues: It often rests standing on just one leg.

A bird that fans out a shimmering blue-green train covered in 'eyes'.

A tiny nectar-drinking bird named after the sound of its fast-beating wings.

The famous extinct flightless bird of the island of Mauritius.
subjects.fact: It is often used as the symbol of extinction, as in the phrase 'dead as a dodo'.

subjects.name: Blue Whale

It feeds by gulping huge mouthfuls of water and filtering out tiny krill.

The ocean predator that terrified beachgoers in the 1975 film Jaws.

A smart, playful sea mammal with a short beak, often seen leaping beside boats.

It lives in the wild on only a few islands of Indonesia.

Lonesome George, the last of his island's kind, died in 2012.

A striped, buzzing insect that makes the sweet golden food we spread on toast.

clues: Despite its common name, it is a beetle and not a true bug.

subjects.fact: The skeleton nicknamed 'Sue' at Chicago's Field Museum is one of the most complete ever found.

clues: It lived in western North America at the same time as one of the most famous predators.
It had a beak like a parrot's and hundreds of grinding teeth.
Its skull could be over 2 metres long, among the biggest of any land animal.
Its name means 'three-horned face'.
A plant-eating dinosaur with a bony neck frill and three horns on its head.
subjects.fact: Some fossils show T. rex bite marks on its frill and horns.

subjects.name: Velociraptor
clues: It was only about the size of a turkey, much smaller than in the movies.
Bumps on its arm bones show it had feathers.

A small, clever hunter made famous by Jurassic Park, whose name means 'swift thief'.

Its spiked tail is nicknamed the 'thagomizer', after a newspaper cartoon.
It is the official state fossil of Colorado.
A plant-eating dinosaur with two rows of tall bony plates along its back.
subjects.fact: More time separates it from T. rex than separates T. rex from us.

It grows wild only in boggy areas of North and South Carolina.
It catches insects to get nutrients missing from its poor soil.
A meat-eating plant whose leaves snap shut like jaws.

subjects.name: Giant Sequoia
clues: Its thick, spongy bark helps it survive forest fires.
Heat from fire helps its cones open and release their seeds.
Some living trees are over 3,000 years old.
It grows naturally only on the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada.
The world's largest tree by volume, like the famous General Sherman.

The tall desert cactus with upturned arms, a classic symbol of the Wild West.

subjects.name: Aurora
clues: It happens when charged particles from the Sun hit gases high in the atmosphere.

It has a southern twin, seen from places such as Tasmania and Antarctica.
Shimmering curtains of colour in the night sky over Norway, Iceland and Canada.

clues: It heats the air to about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
